q: The support system is very important to all living things such as plants, animals and humans.
e: The support system provides essential functions such as maintaining body shape and protecting soft organs.

q: Plants have skeletons like animals that provide support.
e: Plants do not have skeletons; they rely on the turgidity of cells for support.

q: In humans and other animals, the main body support is provided by the internal skeletal system of bones.
e: The internal skeletal system is crucial for support, protection, and enabling movement.

q: Aquatic plants can stay upright on land because of their buoyancy in water.
e: Aquatic plants cannot stay upright on land due to their soft, non-woody stems.

q: The skeleton supports body weight, maintains body shape, and protects soft organs inside the body.
e: These functions are vital for the overall health and functionality of living organisms.

q: Some aquatic plants have many air sacs in their leaves and stems that make them heavy.
e: These air sacs make the plants lighter, enabling them to float on water.

q: The physiological support in plants is a temporary support that depends on the presence of water.
e: Physiological support is crucial for maintaining cell turgidity and overall plant health.

q: The structural support in plants is a temporary support system.
e: Structural support is a permanent support system that helps maintain the plant's shape.

q: Woody plants have specialized tissue to give them support.
e: These specialized tissues include sclerenchyma and xylem, which provide strength.

q: Non-woody plants depend on their roots for structural support.
e: Non-woody plants depend on the turgidity of their cells for structural support.

q: Thorns act as hooks to hold onto support in plants.
e: Thorns are modified branches that provide protection and support.

q: The human skeleton has about 206 bones categorized as axial and appendicular skeleton.
e: This categorization helps in understanding the functions and locations of bones in the body.

q: Cartilage is a rigid connective tissue that protects the ends of bones from wear.
e: Cartilage is a flexible connective tissue that cushions joints and prevents wear.

q: The axial skeleton includes the bones found in the trunk and head of the body.
e: These bones support vital organs and protect the internal structures.

q: The appendicular skeleton is primarily responsible for protecting internal organs.
e: The appendicular skeleton is adapted for movement and locomotion.

q: The skeletal system serves as a storage reservoir for ions such as calcium and phosphorus.
e: This function is essential for maintaining mineral balance in the body.

q: Muscles in the human body work independently to produce movement.
e: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs to produce coordinated movement.

q: The biceps brachii and triceps brachii are an example of antagonistic muscle pairs.
e: These muscles work against each other to allow for flexion and extension of the arm.

q: Plants cannot move from one place to another but can move with their parts.
e: This movement is a response to external stimuli such as light and water.

q: Tropic movements in plants are not dependent on the direction of the stimulus.
e: Tropic movements are directional movements towards or away from a stimulus.

q: Phototropism is the movement of plants in response to light.
e: Plants show positive phototropism in their shoot systems, growing towards light.

q: Geotropism is the movement of a plant part away from the soil.
e: Geotropism is the movement of a plant part towards the soil in response to gravity.

q: Hydrotropism is the movement of the plant towards water.
e: Roots exhibit positive hydrotropism, growing towards moisture.

q: Chemotropism is the movement of plants in response to a physical stimulus.
e: Chemotropism is the movement in response to a chemical stimulus.

q: Thigmotropism is the directional movement in plants in response to touch.
e: Tendrils of climbing plants exhibit thigmotropism by curling around supports.

q: Nastic movements in plants are directional movements.
e: Nastic movements are not directional and occur regardless of the stimulus direction.

q: The leaves of 'touch me not' fold up immediately when touched due to changes in water content.
e: This rapid response is an example of nastic movement.

q: The closing of the lid of the pitcher plant occurs due to the presence of water.
e: The closing occurs due to the catchment of insects, not water.

q: Thermotropism is the movement of plants in response to temperature changes.
e: Plants can adjust their growth based on temperature variations.

q: All types of tropic movements are dependent on the direction of the stimulus.
e: This characteristic defines how plants respond to their environment.

q: Plants exhibit no movement in response to external stimuli.
e: Plants do exhibit movements in response to stimuli such as light and gravity.

q: Tropic movements can be classified into six types, including phototropism and geotropism.
e: These classifications help in understanding plant behavior.

q: Nastic movements are influenced by the direction of the stimulus.
e: Nastic movements occur independently of the stimulus direction.

q: The response of plants to chemicals during fertilization is an example of chemotropism.
e: This demonstrates how plants can respond to chemical signals in their environment.

q: The ability to move in animals is made possible by a combination of a skeletal system and a muscular system.
e: This combination allows for coordinated movement and locomotion.

q: Fish have a streamlined body shape for swimming to increase friction.
e: Fish have a streamlined body shape to reduce friction while swimming.

q: Antagonistic muscle pairs work together to produce movement.
e: Antagonistic muscle pairs work against each other to produce movement.

q: Jumping in grasshoppers is achieved through the contraction of flexor muscles.
e: Jumping is achieved through the contraction of extensor muscles.

q: Frogs use their powerful hind legs for swimming and leaping.
e: These adaptations allow frogs to be effective in both environments.

q: Birds have approximately 100 muscles controlling their wings during flight.
e: Most birds have approximately 175 different muscles controlling their wings.

q: The contraction of the biceps brachii flexes the forearm towards the upper arm.
e: This action is part of the flexion movement at the elbow joint.

q: The quadriceps muscle contracts to flex the leg at the knee.
e: The quadriceps muscle contracts to extend the leg at the knee.

q: Locomotion in fish is achieved through the contraction and relaxation of antagonistic muscles called myotomes.
e: This muscle action allows fish to swim efficiently.

q: Humans have about 500 skeletal muscles in their body.
e: Humans have about 650 skeletal muscles that facilitate movement.

q: The pelvic girdle transmits thrust from the hind legs in frogs during swimming.
e: This helps in propelling the frog forward.

q: Muscular action produces a change in body shape, which does not affect movement.
e: Muscular action directly affects movement by changing body shape.

q: The antagonistic muscle pairs in humans are important for coordinated movement.
e: These pairs allow for smooth and controlled motion.

q: The tail of a fish is used primarily for balance in the water.
e: The tail of a fish is primarily used for propulsion and movement.

q: Birds achieve lift during flight through the contraction of antagonistic muscle pairs.
e: This allows birds to alternate between upstrokes and downstrokes of their wings.

q: The muscles in the human body work independently to produce movement.
e: Muscles work in pairs, with one contracting while the other relaxes to produce movement.
